answer_to_the_commands_question.question: Does the stamp need to be an ancestor, or is a resolvable sha sufficient?
answer_to_the_commands_question.answer: ANCESTOR. The two are different properties and the command is right that only the weaker one survives a shallow clone — so the clone was changed rather than the property. A sha from an abandoned branch resolves perfectly well and describes a state this commit never passed through; 'resolvable' would have accepted it. f5b5810 acted on the ancestor property when it named 4bfbbc5 rather than its own sha, which is the assumption the command stated and it holds.

results.guards: Four. Three on the stamp — not a placeholder, resolves to a commit, is an ancestor of the commit under test — and a fourth on CI's checkout depth.
results.the_fourth_guard_and_why: The ancestry check MUST skip on a shallow clone, because ancestry is unanswerable at fetch-depth 1. A guard that skips in CI forever is a guard that cannot fail, which is the exact class this change exists to close. So test_ci_gives_one_job_the_history_this_guard_needs asserts some CI job checks out with fetch-depth: 0. The skip cannot become permanent without the suite saying so.
results.ci_change: fetch-depth: 0 on the `test` job's checkout, with the reason in the file. The other two jobs are untouched — they run no pytest and need no history.

deviations.what: MY FIRST VERSION OF THIS GUARD COULD NOT FAIL. It passed all three break attempts.
deviations.why: The pattern was `(?:HEAD:|as of)\s*`([0-9a-f]{6,40})``. The header actually reads '**HEAD:** `039cabe`' — markdown bold sits between the label and the sha, so `\s*` matched nothing and findall returned an empty list. Every check below it then iterated over nothing and passed. I wrote a guard that cannot fail INSIDE the change whose purpose is to stop stamps going unchecked.
deviations.how_found: By running the three break attempts and reading the result instead of assuming it. All three printed '3 passed'. That is the only reason this is a deviation and not a shipped defect.
deviations.impact: The pattern now tolerates up to 24 non-backtick characters between label and sha, and the first guard asserts it found AT LEAST TWO stamps before anything else is checked — so a pattern that matches nothing fails loudly instead of vacuously passing. This is the FOURTH time today an instrument or its test could not fail: the preflight pair this morning, the decorative runner test in -009, the _dissent_suffix tests, and now this.

deviations.what: Counts were re-derived, which the command asked not to do as part of this change.
deviations.why: Four new tests move the total, and the count guards are themselves in this file. Not re-deriving would have left the suite red.

questions_for_advisor: Four instruments-that-could-not-fail in one day is no longer a run of bad luck; it is the dominant defect mode of this session. Convention 26 covers an instrument that reports less than it observed. Nothing covers an instrument that reports NOTHING and is read as reporting success. The missing rule is roughly: a guard asserts it FOUND its subject before it asserts anything about it — an empty match set is a failure, never a pass. Three of today's four would have been caught by that alone. I have not written it as a convention because that is the advisor's to rule.

The HEAD stamp reads 039cabe and is ~100 commits behind main. It is a valid ancestor, so the guard passes, and the document's own text says the snapshot is dated 2026-09-13. Should the HEAD stamp track main, or is it deliberately the snapshot's HEAD? If the former, it is drifting silently and the guard cannot see it — ancestry is satisfied by any ancestor, however old.
